about: A toolkit for taking programs apart to study how they work, used by security researchers.

prs.title: Struct views now color addresses by what they point to
prs.broken: The toolkit can lay out memory as a struct, field by field. Fields holding addresses were printed as plain numbers, so you could not tell code from data at a glance, unlike its other memory views.
prs.changed: With colors on, those fields are now colored by the kind of memory they point to: code, writable data or read-only data. Plain and machine-readable output stay the same.
prs.matters: Pointers to code or writable memory stand out while reading a struct.

prs.title: File fingerprints now match the standard ssdeep tool
prs.broken: The toolkit can make a fuzzy fingerprint of a file, used to spot near-copies of malware. Its fingerprints differed from the standard ssdeep tool for many files, and small files got none at all.
prs.changed: The fingerprint is now worked out the same way the standard tool does it, with a fresh start on each pass and the same minimum size.
prs.matters: Researchers can compare the toolkit's fingerprints with ones made anywhere else.

prs.title: The search tool no longer crashes on a badly written pattern
prs.broken: The toolkit's search tool takes patterns written between slashes. Without the slashes, the release version crashed and newer builds silently skipped that search.
prs.changed: The tool now says the pattern is invalid and how to write it, and still runs the other searches.
prs.matters: Users get a clear message instead of a crash or quietly missing results.

prs.title: The hash tool now prints entropy in every output mode
prs.broken: The toolkit's hash tool can measure a file's entropy, a sign of whether data is packed or encrypted. In quiet, JSON and some other modes it printed nothing, or random bytes from memory, instead of the number.
prs.changed: Every output mode now uses one shared step for entropy and the other special cases.
prs.matters: Scripts that ask for entropy in JSON or quiet mode get the real number.

prs.title: The hash tool's JSON mode works for files again
prs.broken: Asking the hash tool for one JSON object per file printed only the file name and nothing else.
prs.changed: The JSON object is now printed for files, the same as for text given on the command line.
prs.matters: Scripts that read the tool's JSON output get the hashes they asked for.

prs.title: The number converter shows the right old-style address
prs.broken: The toolkit's number converter also shows an address in the split format early PCs used. It dropped part of the number, so it showed a different address than the main tool did.
prs.changed: It now uses the same calculation as the main tool.
prs.matters: Both parts of the toolkit agree, and the address shown is the right one.

prs.title: Negative numbers now work with every option of the number converter
prs.broken: Giving the number converter a negative number, like -1, made it ignore the option you asked for, such as decimal output or a size like 'g' for gigabytes, and just print hex.
prs.changed: Negative numbers now go through the same steps as positive ones.
prs.matters: Converting -1 to decimal gives -1, not a long hex number.

prs.title: The number converter now reads every line it is given
prs.broken: Piping several numbers into the number converter, one per line, converted only the first. The line break at the end also confused it, so '1f' came out as 1.
prs.changed: Each line is now cleaned up and converted on its own, as if it were typed separately.
prs.matters: Scripts can feed a whole list of numbers through the converter in one go.

prs.title: Inserting bytes into a file no longer cuts off its end
prs.broken: radare2 lets you insert bytes into a file and push the rest along. With the default settings, the last few bytes fell off the end and were replaced by zeros.
prs.changed: I made the insert move the rest of the file directly, so nothing is lost at the end.
prs.matters: Editing a file this way no longer silently damages it.

prs.title: The file comparison tool shows every change
prs.broken: radare2's tool for comparing two files skipped changes of a single byte, could print random memory for some inputs, and in one mode stopped after the first change.
prs.changed: I fixed how it copies the changed bytes, made it stop reading at the right place, and let it carry on past the first change.
prs.matters: A comparison now lists every difference between the two files, and only what is really there.

prs.title: The assembler's word view shows bytes in the right order
prs.broken: radare2's assembler can print machine code as 4-byte words. For big-endian targets the bytes came out reversed, long output never wrapped, and a short result read past the end of its memory.
prs.changed: I made it read words in the target's byte order, pad the last partial word, and start a new line every eight words.
prs.matters: The word view now matches the real bytes for any target, and short inputs no longer read stray memory.

prs.title: rafind2 reports every match, even back-to-back ones
prs.broken: When a pattern appeared twice in a row, like a run of repeated bytes, rafind2 only reported the first match and dropped the next one with a warning. The r2 search command found them all.
prs.changed: I made rafind2 accept matches that start right where the previous one ended, the same as r2's own search.
prs.matters: A search through a binary no longer hides real hits in repeated data.

prs.title: rahash2 can hash empty files
prs.broken: rahash2 refused any empty file with "Invalid file size", for every hash type, while other tools give the standard hash of empty input.
prs.changed: I made empty files get the same hash as empty input for every algorithm; only a byte range that cannot fit still errors.
prs.matters: Hashing a folder of files no longer fails on the empty ones.

prs.title: rahash2 hashes the same range of every file
prs.broken: When hashing several files with a byte range, rahash2 used that range only for the first file and hashed the rest to the end, so their hashes were wrong.
prs.changed: I made each file get the range that was asked for, while files without a range still use their full size.
prs.matters: Hashing part of many files at once gives the right answer for all of them.

prs.title: rahash2 no longer crashes on empty input
prs.broken: Piping nothing into rahash2 crashed the released version, because it tried to close a file it never opened.
prs.changed: I made it close the file only when one was opened.
prs.matters: Scripts that sometimes pass empty input get a hash instead of a crash.

prs.title: A unit test builds again without network support
prs.broken: When radare2 was built with networking turned off, one of its tests would not compile on newer compilers.
prs.changed: I added the one missing include the test needed.
prs.matters: People building radare2 without networking can run its full test suite.

prs.title: Hashing stops at the end of the file
prs.broken: Asking the hashing tool for a range past the end of a file hashed the last chunk over and over, so the result matched no other tool.
prs.changed: I made the range stop at the file's real size.
prs.matters: A hash of a whole file now matches what standard tools like md5sum print.

prs.title: Block hashes stay inside the range and report read errors
prs.broken: In block mode, the last block could run past the requested end, and a failed read went unnoticed, so the tool hashed stale data.
prs.changed: I made each block stop at the end of the range and made a failed read stop with an error.
prs.matters: Per-block hashes cover exactly the bytes asked for, and a read problem is reported instead of hidden.

prs.title: The number tool reads signed values at the right size
prs.broken: The toolkit's number tool can show a value as a signed number. It guessed the size from the wrong bit, so values like 256 came out as 0 and large numbers came out as -1.
prs.changed: I made it read each value as signed in the smallest of 8, 16, 32 or 64 bits that holds it.
prs.matters: Users converting numbers get the value they typed, not a wrong one.

prs.title: The number tool shows small decimal numbers instead of zero
prs.broken: Converting raw bytes to a decimal number printed only six decimal places, so very small values such as 0.0000001 came out as zero and others lost digits.
prs.changed: The number is now printed with enough digits to get the exact same value back, the way the tool already did for another number format.
prs.matters: People reading values out of a program see what is really stored, not a rounded zero.

prs.title: Changing folders inside the toolkit follows the shell's search list
prs.broken: In a normal terminal, a list of favourite folders lets you jump to a folder by its short name from anywhere. The toolkit's own change-folder command ignored that list, a request open since 2024.
prs.changed: The command now looks the name up in that list the way common shells do, and prints the folder it moved to when the list was used.
prs.matters: People can move around the same way they do in their terminal, including on Windows.
